title: Goa
selection: Goa recorded 9.94 million domestic and 0.47 million foreign tourist visits in 2024, and its two airports handled 1.95% of foreign tourist arrivals by air (India Tourism Data Compendium 2025). Upper Fort Aguada received about 1.36 million domestic visitors in FY 2024-25. Goa was an existing VacayOut record; this file only fills empty fields and adds sections. v2 (2026-11-04): state record rebuilt in the Himachal layout from Goa Tourism (Department of Tourism and GTDC) pages, the Department's Do's and Don'ts, Incredible India and Wikipedia; 13 destination towns added. Goa Tourism's older transport pages are used only for lasting facts — their prices and airline lists are out of date and are not used. Places (2026-11-04): forts (Chapora, Reis Magos, Cabo de Rama), Ponda temples (Mangueshi, Shanta Durga), sanctuaries (Bhagwan Mahavir, Cotigao, Salim Ali, Bondla) and Arvalem falls, from GTDC, Incredible India, the Goa Forest Department and Wikipedia. Opening hours only where Incredible India lists them; Cotigao's listed hours are inconsistent and are left out; the Forest Department's Dudhsagar notice is from 2015–16 and is not used. No entry fees were confirmed. Things to do (2026-11-04): GTDC's adventure, market, shopping and drinks pages, Incredible India's adventure guide and Wikipedia (casinos). Prices appear only where GTDC lists them, labelled as estimates; GTDC flags that its market listings may be out of date.

places.name: Goa
places.summary: India's smallest state: busy North Goa beaches, calm South Goa bays, the UNESCO churches of Old Goa, Portuguese-era Panaji and a forested hinterland with Dudhsagar Falls.
places.seoTitle: Goa Travel Guide: Beaches, Old Goa Churches & Food
places.seoDescription: Plan a Goa trip: North and South Goa beaches, the UNESCO churches of Old Goa, Panaji, Fort Aguada, Dudhsagar Falls, Goan food, getting there and the best season.

overview.text:
Goa is India's smallest state, a 103-km strip of coast between Maharashtra and Karnataka, cut off from the Deccan by the forested Western Ghats. For four and a half centuries it was the capital of Portugal's eastern empire, and that history still shows in its whitewashed churches, old Latin quarters and food. It recorded 9.94 million domestic and 0.47 million foreign tourist visits in 2024.

Most trips are built around the beaches. North Goa is the busy side — Candolim, Calangute and Baga run as one long beach, with Anjuna's flea market and Vagator's cliffs beyond, and the quieter Pernem beaches of Morjim, Mandrem and Arambol up to the Maharashtra border. South Goa is calmer: the broad sands of Colva and Benaulim near Margao, and the bays of Palolem and Agonda in the far south.

Away from the sea, the churches of Old Goa are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, Panaji's Fontainhas quarter keeps its painted houses, Ponda has Goa's great temples, and the Western Ghats hold wildlife sanctuaries and the 310-metre Dudhsagar Falls.

best_time.text:
November–February: dry, sunny and the main beach season; December to February is the peak, and Christmas to New Year is the busiest week of the year — book rooms well ahead.

March–May: hot and humid; noon temperatures often pass 33°C in May. Shigmo falls in March or April.

June–September: the monsoon. June and July each bring around 900 mm of rain at Panaji. The sea is rough with dangerous undercurrents — don't swim — and water sports stop, but the hinterland turns green and Dudhsagar and Arvalem falls are at their fullest. São João is on 24 June and Bonderam in late August.

October: the rain tails off (about 156 mm) and the season begins. November–December brings the International Film Festival of India.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: Goa has two airports. Manohar International at Mopa, in Pernem, opened in January 2023 and is about 40 km from Panaji — closest for the northern beaches. Dabolim, near Vasco da Gama in the south, is about 30 km from Panaji. They are about 60 km apart. Goa Tourism advises booking early for October to January, when flights run full.

By rail: the Konkan Railway runs along the coast; Goa's main stations are Margao (Madgaon Junction), the Konkan Railway terminus, and Vasco da Gama. Mumbai–Goa trains take about 8–12 hours, and trains often run full, so reserve ahead.

By road: NH-66 follows the coast to Mumbai and Mangalore, and NH-4A climbs to Belagavi. Kadamba Transport Corporation and private operators run interstate buses from the Kadamba bus stand in Panaji; Mumbai is about 12–16 hours by bus.

By sea: there is no passenger service — the last Mumbai–Goa sea route stopped in 2004.

items.body: November to February for dry, sunny beach days; December to February is the peak. March to May is hot. June to September is the monsoon — green and quiet, but the sea is unsafe for swimming.

items.title: North Goa or South Goa?
items.body: North Goa — Calangute, Baga, Anjuna, Vagator — is busy, with water sports and nightlife. South Goa — Colva, Benaulim, Palolem, Agonda — is calmer and quieter.

items.title: How do I get around Goa?
items.body: By taxi (white tourist taxis or motorcycle 'pilots' — agree the fare first), by local bus from hubs like Mapusa and Margao, or by hired scooter.

items.body: No. Drinking, drugs and smoking are banned on all beaches and punishable with a fine or jail.

items.title: Is it safe to swim in Goa?
items.body: Yes, in season and between the red-and-yellow flags watched by lifesavers. Don't swim in the monsoon, after dark or after drinking.

items.title: Which trains go to Goa?
items.body: Konkan Railway trains stop at Margao (Madgaon Junction), the main station for South Goa; Vasco da Gama is the other main station. Mumbai–Goa trains take about 8–12 hours.

overview.text:
Panaji (Panjim), Goa's capital, sits at the mouth of the Mandovi river. The Portuguese viceroy moved here from Old Goa in 1759 after a series of epidemics, and in 1843 it became the official capital of Portuguese India.

Its landmark is the Church of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, built in 1619, with a double flight of stairs added in 1871. The former Institute Vasco da Gama, now Goa's Central Library, has a 1935 mural of blue azulejo tiles depicting Os Lusíadas. Wander the narrow lanes and colourful houses of Fontainhas, then head to Miramar beach, 3 km west, or Dona Paula, 7 km south-west, for views across the bay.

overview.text:
Old Goa was the capital of Portuguese India and a centre of missionary activity from the 16th century. Its churches and convents became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

The highlights are close together: the Basilica of Bom Jesus, holding the remains of St Francis Xavier; the vast Se Cathedral, begun in 1562; the Church of Our Lady of the Rosary, from 1543 the oldest church still standing here; and the Church of St Francis of Assisi. The Archaeological Museum and the ruins of the Church of St Augustine complete a half-day visit.

overview.text:
The Basilica of Bom Jesus — 'Good Jesus' — was built between 1594 and 1605 and is part of Old Goa's UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its black granite facade blends Doric, Corinthian and composite styles, and Pope Pius XII made it a minor basilica in 1946.

Inside, a chapel holds the remains of St Francis Xavier in a silver casket; every 10 years they are lowered for a public exposition that draws pilgrims from around the world. Next door, the Professed House of the Jesuits, from 1585, is older than the basilica itself.

overview.text:
Fort Aguada was built by the Portuguese in 1612 to guard the mouth of the Mandovi against the Dutch. A freshwater spring inside gave it its name — 'aguada' means watery — and ships stopped here to take on water. The upper fort stored water and defended the coast, while the lower part sheltered Portuguese ships, with a moat and an underground gunpowder room.

The old lighthouse dates from 1864 and was replaced by a newer one in 1976. The fort is about 18 km from Panaji, above Sinquerim and Candolim beaches. It is one of Goa's most visited monuments: in 2024–25 Upper Fort Aguada received about 1.36 million domestic and 13,025 foreign visitors.

overview.text: Anjuna drew free-spirited hippies in the 1960s and later became famous for trance parties. Unlike most Goan beaches, its shore is lined with rugged rocks that jut into the sea and form small coves. Every Wednesday the Anjuna flea market sells handicrafts, clothes, jewellery and spices. On a hill nearby, Chapora Fort looks out over Anjuna and Vagator beaches. Today the village mixes its bohemian past with cafés, resorts and water sports; Incredible India suggests November to February as the best time to visit.

overview.text:
Dudhsagar — 'Sea of Milk' — is a four-tiered waterfall on the Mandovi (Mahadayi) river, and at 310 metres one of India's tallest. It lies in the Western Ghats inside the Bhagwan Mahaveer Sanctuary and Mollem National Park, about 60 km from Panaji by road and 46 km east of Madgaon, beside the railway line to Belagavi.

The falls are at their fullest in the monsoon. The surrounding 240 sq km park is home to around 120 bird species, and the 12th-century Tambdi Surla temple, known for its stone carving, is nearby.

Baga sits 2 km north of Calangute, at the end of the long beach that starts at Sinquerim. It takes its name from Baga Creek, which meets the sea at the north end of the sand.

This is the place for water sports — jet skis, parasailing, banana boats — and for boat trips to look for dolphins 1–2 km offshore. Boats also go up the creek through the mangroves. After dark the shacks fill with music, and every Saturday the night market opens.

Vagator is a curving bay about 22 km from Panaji, running from the headland to the hill crowned by Chapora Fort. Red laterite cliffs divide it into Big Vagator and Little Vagator, and it is less crowded than Baga and Calangute.

Palolem, in Canacona in the far south, is a gentle arc of palm-lined sand facing a sheltered bay — one of Goa's safest places to swim, kayak and paddleboard. In season the beach fills with bamboo huts and palm-thatch restaurants.

Loud music stops at 10 pm, which is why Palolem became known for headphone 'silent noise' parties. Fishermen take boats out to spot dolphins, best early in the morning, and quiet Patnem is next door. Cotigao Wildlife Sanctuary is a short drive inland.

Today it is a ruin — the church of St Anthony has gone and the open ground inside is a tumble of stones — but the walls give wide views over Anjuna, Vagator and the sea. The film Dil Chahta Hai made it famous.

overview.text:
The Shri Manguesh temple at Mangueshi in Priol, Ponda taluka, is one of Goa's largest and most visited temples, 21 km from Panaji and 26 km from Margao. The deity, a form of Shiva, was moved here from Cortalim in 1560 when the Portuguese began conversions in Salcete.

Legend says Shiva became a tiger to frighten Parvati, who cried 'Trahi Mam Girisha' — the phrase that gave Manguesh its name. Inside, a hall for over 500 people hangs with 19th-century chandeliers, and every Monday the deity is carried out in a palanquin procession.

Her original temple at Quelossim in Salcete was destroyed by the Portuguese in 1564, and worship moved to Kavalem. The present temple was built between 1730 and 1738, in the reign of the Maratha ruler Shahu, and renovated in 1966.

Bhagwan Mahavir Sanctuary is Goa's largest protected area — 240 sq km of Western Ghats forest on the Karnataka border, 57 km east of Panaji, with Mollem National Park at its core. It became a sanctuary in 1969, and its core was declared a national park in 1978. NH-4A and the railway to Londa pass through it.

Inside are Dudhsagar Falls, the 12th-century Tambdi Surla temple and Devil's Canyon. Gaur, sambar, leopards and spotted deer live here, though you may not see them on a first visit; birders come for its many species.

Cotigao, set up in 1968, is Goa's southernmost protected area: 86 sq km of forest in Canacona, about 2 km from Poinguinim and a short drive from Palolem. Its best-known feature is a treetop watchtower 25 m above a waterhole — go at dawn or dusk, when animals come to drink.

Eight nature trails run from 500 m to 5 km. Look for the black leopard, sloth bear, flying squirrel, slender loris and Indian pied hornbill. Velip and Kunbil communities live around the sanctuary, and the Parshurama temple and Kuskem waterfall are nearby.

overview.text:
The Dr Salim Ali Bird Sanctuary covers 1.8 sq km of mangrove estuary at the western tip of Chorao island on the Mandovi. Reach it by ferry from Ribandar, near Panaji. A paved walk runs through the mangroves, and at high tide the canals are explored by boat.

Look for striated and western reef herons, white egrets and purple herons; marsh crocodiles are sometimes seen. Go early in the morning, then hire a bike to explore Chorao's quiet lanes and eat a Goan fish thali at a home-run eatery.

Beginners need no experience. Divers must be at least 10; children aged 5–10 can ride along on the boat, but under-5s are not allowed. Fill in the medical form before you book.

overview.text:
The busy North Goa beaches are where the water sports are. Calangute, Anjuna and Baga are the popular parasailing beaches; Baga adds jet skis, banana boats and bumper boats, and Candolim is known for parasailing and water skiing. Paragliding runs on beaches in both North and South Goa, with Arambol a hub.

Stay inside the black-and-white chequered flags while you are on the water. Prices vary between operators, so agree the price first and bargain a little. In the June–September monsoon the sea is rough with dangerous undercurrents.

overview.text:
Goa's permanent bungee site is at Mayem Lake in North Goa, 35 minutes' drive from Baga: a 55-metre jump run by Jumpin Heights to Australian and New Zealand safety standards. It runs all year except the monsoon, mid-June to mid-August.

The monsoon is the time for white-water rafting on the Mhadei, run by Southern River Adventures with GTDC from June to October — it only runs when it rains. You don't need to swim, but nobody over 120 kg can go, and you must book ahead. For a calmer view, hot-air balloon flights take off early in the morning from Chandor.

overview.text:
Goa has a long tradition of weekly markets. The best known is Anjuna's Wednesday flea market, along the beach from about 10 am to 4 pm, selling clothes, jewellery, handicrafts and spices. North Goa also has three night markets — Mackie's Saturday Night Bazaar on Baga creek and two at Arpora, with food from around the world — and at Arambol vendors spread their work on the sand at sunset.

For local produce, go to Mapusa's Friday market. Bargain on non-essentials, watch your bags and check purchases before you leave.

places.seoDescription: Goa nightlife: where to go out (Calangute–Baga, Assagao, Vagator, Palolem), the Mandovi floating casinos, and the beach-alcohol and drug laws to know.

overview.text:
Calangute–Baga is Goa's main nightlife strip, and Baga has the busiest night scene; some places in Assagao hold special nights during the week. Little Vagator's clifftop bars draw a sunset crowd, while in Palolem loud music stops at 10 pm and parties go silent, on headphones.

Casinos are legal in Goa in five-star hotels and on offshore vessels — the floating casinos are moored on the Mandovi at Panaji and reached by feeder boats.

Know the rules: drinking is banned on beaches, and drug offences are non-bailable, with sentences from 6 months to 30 years.

places.seoTitle: Goan Food & Shopping: What to Eat, Drink and Buy
places.seoDescription: What to eat and drink in Goa — fish curry rice, thalis, feni, urrak, sol kadi — and what to buy: cashews, masalas, bebinca, and crafts from government Aparanta stores.

images.commons: File:Goan typical meal -- fish, curry and rice.jpg
images.alt: A Goan thali with rice, fish curry, fried fish and vegetables on a steel plate
images.caption: A Goan fish curry rice meal

overview.text:
Rice with fish curry is Goa's everyday staple, and old Goan eateries serve vegetarian and non-vegetarian thalis; bhaji with pao makes a filling local meal. Feni is the local spirit, sold all year; urrak, from the first distillation of cashew fruit, is drunk only in summer, and fresh cashew juice (niro) is best from March to May. Finish a meal with sol kadi, made from coconut milk or kokum.

To take home: cashews, local masalas, a bottle of feni, and sweets such as bebinca, bolinha and guava cheese; for crafts, try the government-run Aparanta stores. In July and August, Goa Tourism runs a monsoon Gastronomy Month.
